strengths: Clear and well-motivated positioning: lifting LLM-driven heuristic design from the heuristic level to the optimizer level (outer meta-optimization loop over inner heuristic-evolution loop) is a sensible and novel step beyond EoH/ReEvo/HSEvo/MCTS-AHD, and the paper clearly articulates the two limitations (fixed EC optimizer, single-task training) it addresses.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: TSP (constructive and improvement/GLS/KGLS variants), online BPP, plus additional CVRP, offline BPP, and TSPLib results in the appendix, against strong and up-to-date LLM-based baselines rerun under identical budgets, as well as traditional and neural solvers.

MoH consistently achieves the best or near-best results across settings, with the most visible gains in cross-size generalization (Fig. 1) and online BPP (average 0.453% vs 0.680% for the best baseline), supporting the multi-task training claim.

Good analysis and transparency: ablations on idea generation and population size, evaluation across four different LLMs, a detailed computational cost comparison (tokens, LLM requests, wall-clock time) showing MoH is actually cheaper than several baselines despite the extra outer loop, and interpretable examples of evolved meta-optimizers (ACO, PSO, Tabu, hybrid strategies) in the appendix.
Reproducibility commitments (code/data release), license declarations, and a clear description of the algorithm and prompts sufficient for reimplementation.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental rather than groundbreaking: the recursive/self-improving optimizer idea closely follows STOP [87] and prompt-optimization works [91], applied here to the LLM-EC heuristic-design pipeline; the two-loop architecture is a natural extension rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Headline gains in the main improvement-heuristic setting are small and possibly within run-to-run variance: average gap 0.391% vs 0.411% (MCTS-AHD) and 0.466% (ReEvo/HSEvo); no statistical significance tests or variance bars are reported for the main tables (only 3 runs of the best heuristic).

Dependence on the specific LLM (GPT-4o-mini) and its behavior; the framework's outcomes (which optimizers are discovered) may not be stable across LLM versions, and the ablation shows non-trivial sensitivity (e.g., o1-mini underperforms 4o-mini at scale) without a deeper explanation.

Some potential confounds in the meta-optimizer evaluation: candidate optimizers are selected using a best-of-population utility on validation instances, which risks overfitting the validation set; no held-out validation/test separation or discussion of selection bias is provided.

Claims of 'state-of-the-art' are supported mainly on classic COPs with specific settings; the search-efficiency limitation acknowledged by the authors (roughly 2x baseline cost for CVRP, higher per-iteration cost) is not fully quantified in the main text and the multi-task scheme's benefit versus simply training a strong single-task optimizer per task size is not directly ablated.

Comparisons to a broader family of alternatives (e.g., algorithm configuration/selection methods, or a simple random search over optimizers) are missing, making it hard to attribute gains specifically to the learned meta-optimizer rather than the extra compute spent on optimizer search.

strengths: The proposed two-level optimization framework (outer loop for optimizer design, inner loop for heuristic design) is a sensible and well-motivated extension of existing LLM-EC approaches, and the multi-task training scheme addresses a real generalization limitation of prior work.

The empirical evaluation is broad: TSP (constructive and improvement heuristics), online BPP, plus additional CVRP, offline BPP, and TSPLib results, with many strong baselines (FunSearch, EoH, ReEvo, HSEvo, MCTS-AHD, Concorde, OR-Tools, neural solvers) rerun under identical budgets.

Ablations cover LLM choice, idea generation, and population size, and a cost analysis (token usage, LLM requests, wall-clock time) is provided, which is more transparent than most papers in this line of work.
The paper includes qualitative analysis of generated meta-optimizers (GA, ACO, PSO, Tabu Search, hybrids), supporting the interpretability claim, and the authors promise code and data release.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the outer loop is essentially EoH-style evolutionary search applied one level up, and recursive LLM self-improvement of optimizer code is very close to STOP [87]. The claim of 'eliminating reliance on a predefined EC optimizer' is overstated, since the seed optimizer (Fig. 8) is itself a hand-designed fixed procedure, and the generated meta-optimizers largely re-instantiate classical metaheuristics.

Gains over the strongest baselines are small and possibly within noise: in the improvement-heuristic setting, MoH-KGLS (0.391%) beats MCTS-AHD-KGLS (0.411%) by a margin that is unlikely to be statistically significant, yet results are reported as best-of-3 runs with no significance testing or variance reporting.

The higher computational cost of the extra outer loop is not convincingly justified: MoH-Train uses more tokens/time than EoH/HSEvo in Table 8, and the multi-task setting further multiplies inner-loop evaluations, weakening the efficiency story.

Methodological concerns about overfitting to the validation set are not addressed: the meta-optimizer is selected by utility on validation datasets, and there is no analysis of validation/test overlap, dataset size sensitivity, or selection bias across three runs.

The generalization claim rests on very few tasks (e.g., only two BPP training settings; four TSP sizes), and 'multi-task' training here is essentially just cross-size instance mixing, so claims of broad generalization capability are stronger than the evidence.

Inspection of the example meta-optimizers suggests weak correctness: e.g., the PSO example performs arithmetic ('-') on solution strings, and several examples are essentially classical metaheuristics with LLM calls bolted on, which undercuts the claim of 'novel optimization strategies'.

Dependence on a specific proprietary LLM (GPT-4o-mini snapshot) limits reproducibility, and behavior of the framework is admitted to vary with LLM version, undermining confidence in the reported numbers being stable.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and relevant gap in LLM-based heuristic design: existing LLM-EC frameworks (EoH, ReEvo, HSEvo, MCTS-AHD) fix the EC optimizer, and MoH lifts the search to the optimizer level via an iterative meta-optimization loop. This is a sensible and well-motivated abstraction, and the distinction between outer-loop (optimizer design) and inner-loop (heuristic design) is clearly formalized in Eq. (2) and Algorithm 1.

The empirical evaluation is extensive and mostly convincing: TSP constructive and improvement (GLS/KGLS) settings, online BPP, plus additional CVRP, offline BPP, and TSPLib results in the appendix. MoH consistently beats strong recent baselines (EoH, ReEvo, HSEvo, MCTS-AHD, FunSearch) under a matched evaluation budget of 1,000 heuristic evaluations, and generalization to larger instance sizes (e.g., TSP1000, TSPLib up to size 1000) is a concrete strength.

The paper is commendably transparent about computational cost: Tables 8 and 9 report time, token usage, LLM request counts, and evaluation counts, showing MoH is not simply winning by spending more compute (e.g., it uses fewer total tokens than EoH on TSP-GLS and ReEvo/HSEvo on CVRP).

Useful ablations are provided: different LLMs (4o-mini, o1-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-Plus) to show framework robustness, idea generation vs. pure code sampling, and population size effects, with convergence curves in Fig. 4.

Qualitative analysis of the discovered meta-optimizers (GA, ACO, PSO, Simulated Annealing, Tabu Search, hybrid strategies in Appendix D) supports the claim that the framework discovers interpretable, diverse optimization strategies beyond a fixed EC workflow, which is the core claimed contribution.

Reproducibility signals are reasonable: prompts, seed optimizer code, optimizer signature, and generated examples are all included in the appendix, code/datasets are promised for release, and licenses of all used assets are documented.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: optimizing the optimizer is closely related to prior self-improving code-generation work, notably STOP (Zelikman et al., 2024, cited as [87]) and prompt-optimization/self-refinement methods ([91], [32]). The main deltas are (a) recursive self-invocation applied to EC-style optimizers and (b) multi-task training. The paper could better position and differentiate its contribution against these works rather than framing the outer loop as fully novel.

Margins over the strongest baselines are small in the most competitive setting: for TSP-KGLS, MoH achieves 0.391% average gap vs. 0.411% for MCTS-AHD, and for TSP-GLS 0.453% vs. 0.464% (ReEvo/HSEvo) — differences of a few hundredths of a percent. The paper reports best-of-three-runs performance in the main tables, which introduces a selection bias favoring the proposed method; per-run variance or statistical significance tests are not reported.

Dependence on a single commercial LLM (GPT-4o-mini, 2024-07-18) as the primary model raises reproducibility concerns: results are tied to a specific versioned API model that may be deprecated, and exact behavior of the meta-optimizer is acknowledged to vary with prompts and LLM versions.

The multi-task training scheme, one of the two claimed contributions, is under-analyzed: task weights wi are introduced in Eq. (2) but never ablated, there is no comparison against alternative multi-task strategies (e.g., task-conditioned prompting vs. separate heuristic populations), and the invocation of the No Free Lunch Theorem to motivate the design is superficial.

Increased complexity of the two-level search is only partially mitigated: MoH-Train takes 238 minutes vs. 326 for EoH on TSP-GLS (favorable), but the added outer loop increases variance in what strategies are discovered, and the paper itself concedes search efficiency is a limitation. A deeper analysis of when/why the meta-optimizer actually improves over a well-tuned fixed optimizer (e.g., budget-matched EoH with more iterations) would strengthen the case.

Some presentation issues remain: typos ('generats', 'acorss'), and the formulation in Sec. 4.1 conflates notation between heuristic-level and optimizer-level objectives at times. The discovered meta-optimizers in Appendix D include constructs that are only loosely meaningful (e.g., PSO 'velocity' computed by subtracting code strings), which is acceptable as LLM output but somewhat undermines the 'interpretable optimizer' narrative without additional scrutiny.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and relevant limitation of existing LLM-EC frameworks (fixed heuristic-optimizer, single-task training) and proposes a well-motivated meta-optimization framework (MoH) that searches over the space of optimization strategies rather than heuristics alone.
The problem formulation is clean: the bilevel objective (Eq. 2) with task-weighted utility is clearly stated, and Algorithm 1 makes the outer/inner loop workflow easy to follow.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this line of work: TSP (constructive and improvement settings), online/offline BPP, CVRP, TSPLib, cross-size and cross-distribution generalization, cross-problem preliminary experiments, additional domains (QAP, Acrobot), ablations (idea generation, population size, multiple LLMs), cost/token analysis under matched evaluation budgets, statistical significance tests, and repeated-run variance reporting.

Cost analysis (Tables 10-12) shows MoH actually uses fewer tokens and LLM requests than several baselines at comparable or better performance, which preempts the natural objection that the extra meta-level simply buys performance with more compute.

The appendix provides concrete, inspectable examples of generated meta-optimizers (GA, ACO, PSO, SA+DE, Tabu, hybrid strategies), supporting the interpretability claim and demonstrating that the framework discovers diverse strategies beyond EC.

Results are consistent: MoH is best or near-best in nearly all settings, with the largest gains appearing exactly where the paper's motivation lies (cross-size generalization to large instances, e.g., 1.889% vs 3.26-3.49% for baselines at TSP1000).
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than groundbreaking: MoH is essentially an additional evolutionary loop placed above existing LLM-EC pipelines, with the same ingredient set (LLM-generated code, population management, utility-driven selection). The framing as 'meta-optimization' or 'bi-level optimization' is largely repackaging, and the strongest objection-that this is meta-prompt/algorithm search over the same search primitives-is only partially answered.

Improvements in the improvement-heuristic settings are small in absolute terms (e.g., MoH-KGLS 0.391% vs MCTS-AHD-KGLS 0.411% average gap; several TSPLib rows are identical across methods), so the headline SOTA claim rests partly on a few larger-size settings.

The framework's success appears sensitive to the seed meta-optimizer and prompt design (Fig. 5, 8), but there is no ablation over seed meta-optimizers or prompt variants, so the robustness of the outer loop's contribution is not fully isolated from prompt engineering effects.

Evaluation on the improvement settings inherits the GLS/KGLS scaffold; the paper does not test whether meta-optimization helps when the downstream optimizer itself is weaker or more varied, which would strengthen the generality claim.

Some fairness concerns remain: MoH gets an outer loop with additional optimizer-level search; while evaluation counts are budgeted at 1,000, the number of LLM calls and total optimizer-level search differs across methods, and the interaction between outer-loop budget and performance is not systematically explored (only T=10 is used).
The code availability link is incomplete in the submitted version, which weakens reproducibility despite the detailed appendix.

strengths: The paper addresses a natural and well-motivated gap: existing LLM-EC heuristic design frameworks (EoH, ReEvo, HSEvo, MCTS-AHD) fix the outer optimization loop, and MoH instead searches over the optimizer itself, which is a coherent conceptual step.

The empirical evaluation is broad: TSP (constructive and improvement), online/offline BPP, CVRP, TSPLib, plus auxiliary tasks (QAP, Acrobot), with comparisons to classical solvers (Concorde, OR-Tools) and neural solvers (POMO, LEHD, SIL, NeuOpt).
Computational cost is transparently reported (token counts, LLM requests, wall-clock time), which is uncommon and valuable for this line of work.
The appendix provides reproducibility support: prompts, seed and generated meta-optimizers, licenses, and multiple ablations (idea generation, population size, choice of LLM).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The core idea—using an LLM to iteratively rewrite its own optimizer/prompt program—is very close to STOP (Zelikman et al., 2024, which the authors cite) and to classical hyper-heuristics; the contribution largely amounts to wrapping an existing LLM-EC loop in one additional LLM-driven selection loop. The bi-level framing in Eq. (2) is a formalization, not a new mechanism.

Gains in the practically most relevant setting are marginal. In the improvement-heuristic (KGLS) setting, MoH achieves 0.391% average gap versus 0.411% for MCTS-AHD-KGLS and 0.466% for ReEvo-KGLS—differences within what three runs and selection noise plausibly explain. Reporting the best of three independent runs (rather than, e.g., mean with significance per comparison) further weakens these small margins.

The constructive-heuristic results, while numerically better than baselines (11.79% vs ~12.5-13.4%), remain far behind even OR-Tools (2.01%), so the practical significance of the improvement is unclear.

Insufficient isolation of where gains come from. The claimed two contributions—meta-optimization and multi-task training—are entangled. The ablations (idea generation, population size, LLM choice) do not include the most important one: MoH with a fixed EC optimizer in the outer loop vs. learned meta-optimizers under the same budget, which would directly test the central claim.

Added complexity and overhead are acknowledged but not convincingly justified: the outer/inner loop multiplies LLM invocations and evaluations, and Table 11 shows MoH-Train uses substantially more resources than the budget-limited baselines, complicating the 'same budget' fairness claim.

Some methodological details are opaque or delegated entirely to the appendix: population management, utility weighting wi ∝ si, inference-time seed direction generation (Fig. 7), and the 'judgment mechanisms' mentioned in D.1 are described only loosely, hurting reproducibility.

The statistical significance tests (Table 15) compare objective values of heuristics from the best runs, which conflate instance-level variance with run-level selection effects; a more appropriate test at the run level is not provided.

The paper's framing overstates the contribution ('state-of-the-art', 'a step beyond previous LLM-EC design') relative to what the evidence supports, particularly given the near-ties with MCTS-AHD under KGLS.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: lifting the search from heuristics to heuristic-optimizers (meta-optimizers) in LLM-based heuristic design is a conceptually meaningful step beyond fixed LLM-EC pipelines like EoH, ReEvo, HSEvo, and MCTS-AHD.

Comprehensive evaluation across multiple problems (TSP constructive/improvement, online/offline BPP, CVRP, plus QAP and Acrobot), multiple LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, o1-mini, DeepSeek-v3, Qwen-plus), and both cross-size and cross-distribution (TSPLib, uniform-to-cluster) settings.

Strong empirical results, particularly on cross-size generalization (e.g., average optimality gap 11.792% constructive, 0.391% MoH-KGLS, outperforming all rerun baselines), with statistical significance tests (Wilcoxon) and mean±std reporting across runs.
Transparent computational cost analysis (Tables 10-13) showing MoH's token/time budgets are comparable to or lower than baselines, plus ablations on idea generation, population size, and LLM choice.
Good reproducibility posture: code release promised, detailed prompt design (Appendix D), seed and generated meta-optimizer examples (Appendix E), and license/asset disclosure.
The FAQ section (Appendix A) proactively addresses positioning versus multi-task, multi-objective, bi-level optimization, and meta-prompt optimization, which strengthens the novelty argument.
weaknesses: Marginal absolute gains in some headline settings: e.g., MoH-KGLS 0.391% vs. MCTS-AHD-KGLS 0.411% average gap, and comparable results on several TSPLib instances; the improvement-heuristic advantage over the strongest baseline is thin even if statistically significant.

Novelty is somewhat incremental over existing ideas: recursive self-improvement of code-generating optimizers (STOP, Zelikman et al. 2024) and LLM-EC frameworks are known; the contribution is essentially applying a (self-)invocation outer loop with multi-task weighting to heuristic design, and the framework definition (Eq. 2) is informal rather than theoretically grounded.

The 'training' relies on a closed-source commercial LLM (GPT-4o-mini, 2024-07-18) whose behavior may change over time, weakening long-term reproducibility; results are also reported on the best of three independent runs in some tables, which inflates apparent performance.

The meta-optimization introduces additional hyperparameters and complexity (outer iterations, M and K, population sizes, task weights w_i = s_i/Σs_j) with limited justification; the size-weighted utility is ad hoc and ablated only weakly.

Potential confound: MoH's gains may partly stem from effectively using more LLM calls/evaluations in the inner loop via diverse optimizers; the evaluation-budget matching is approximate, and no ablation isolates the outer loop against a strong fixed-optimizer baseline under identical inner-loop budgets.

Scope limited to classical routing/packing COPs with hand-crafted utility functions; cross-problem generalization is admittedly weak (preliminary Table 6 only), so the claimed 'generalizability' is narrower than the framing suggests.
